sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Yammu** ​(*yammu*) — ‌The Sea, ‌Rival ​of Baʿal ​· Sea ​— ​belongs to ​the Phoenician ‌tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Sea, Chaos". ​The name ‌means ​"Sea"[^1].

**Yammu** ​is the ​Canaanite ​sea-god: the ​personified ocean ‌whose ​rebellion against ‌the divine ​council ‌set the ​Baal Cycle ‌in ​motion, and ‌whose defeat ​by ​Baʿal — ‌with two ‌magic clubs ‌thrown ​from the ​storm-cloud — ‌established ​the storm-god’s ​kingship over ‌the ​gods. The ​Ugaritic tablets ‌of ​the fourteenth ‌century BCE, ​found ​in 1929, ​gave him ​back ‌his name ‌after three ​thousand ‌years of ​silence.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores the ‌name ‌as **Yammu** ‌and serves ‌its ​temple at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/yammu/). ​The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ‌a ​description computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ​form *yammu* ‌survives as ​a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, not ​the ​fallback, is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested ​in ​Phoenician ​as **𐤉𐤌**. ​Etymologically ​it ‌means ​"Sea"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII ​form ‌*yammu* ​survives ‌only ​because the ​early ​domain-name ​system ​could ‌not ​carry ‌diacritics; ​it ‌is ​a ‌technological compromise, ​not ‌an ​ancient ​spelling. ‌The ‌Unicode ‌restoration ​**Yammu** ​recovers ‌the ​full diacritic ​detail ‌of ​the ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​directly ‌in ​the ​address ​bar. ​The restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent ‌form ​— ‌a ​description ​computed ‌from ‌the ‌displayed ‌form ​itself.

The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ​**y** ‌→ ​**Y** ​— ​Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**a** ​→ **a** ​— ‌Same
- ​**m** ‌→ ​**m** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**m** ‌→ ​**m** ​— Same
- ​**u** ​→ ‌**u** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the ​name is ​**/ˈjɑːmʊ/** ​— Ugaritic ​(conventional ​vocalisation).[^1]

‌Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ​**Ym** ‌— Written ​ym ‌in Ugaritic ​cuneiform; ‌conventionally ​vocalised “Yammu”. ​The ​word means ​“sea”.
- ​**** ‌— The ​Canaanite ‌sea-god, ​rival and ‌enemy ​of Baʿal, ‌defeated ​in ‌the great ​Baal ​Cycle of ‌Ugarit.
- ‌**** ‌— The ​name ​needs ‌no vowels ​the ​Ugaritic scribes ‌would ​not ​have recognised ‌— ​a plain ‌transliteration.

​For ​the modern ​speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation ‌is: ​“YAH-moo”

Kindred ‌and ​historical ​forms of ‌the ‌name:

- **Akkadian** ‌— ‌Tiamat’s ​kin — ‌the ​sea-monster of ​the ​Enūma ‌eliš
- **Rival** ​— ​Baal ​(Baʿlu) — ‌the ​storm-god of ​the ​Ugaritic ‌tablets

He ​is ‌the sea ​itself ‌as ​god: the ‌oldest ‌named ​enemy in ​the ​Baal Cycle, ​defeated ‌at ‌the world’s ​beginning.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Yammu** ​is the ‌Canaanite sea-god: ‌the ​personified ocean ​whose ​rebellion against ​the divine ​council ‌set the ​Baal ​Cycle in ‌motion, and ​whose ‌defeat by ​Baʿal — ‌with ​two magic ​clubs ​thrown from ​the storm-cloud ​— ‌established the ​storm-god’s ‌kingship over ​the gods. ‌The ​Ugaritic tablets ‌of ​the fourteenth ‌century BCE, ​found ​in 1929, ‌gave him ‌back ‌his name ​after ​three thousand ‌years of ​silence.[^1]

### ​The Sea ‌Itself

​His name ​IS the ‌word ​“sea” (ym) ‌— the ​ocean ​as the ​first ​rebel against ‌order.

### The ‌Two ​Clubs

“Chaser” ‌and ​“Driver”, the ​magic clubs ‌Baʿal ‌threw to ‌shatter his ‌skull ​— the ‌cycle’s ​most quoted ​scene.

### The ​Divine ‌Council

He ​demanded ​Baʿal’s surrender ​from the ‌council ​of El; ​the ​gods’ cowardice ‌set the ​war ‌in motion.

### ​The Tablet’s ‌Return

​Found at ‌Ugarit ‌(Ras Shamra) ​in 1929 ​— ​the Baal ​Cycle ‌restored Canaanite ‌religion to ​history.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Yammu ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set ‌of recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a ​compressed ‌statement ​about ‌the name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Sea ​Itself** ​— ​His ‌name IS ​the ‌word ​“sea” ‌(ym) ​— ‌the ocean ​as ‌the ​first ​rebel ‌against ‌order.
- ‌**The Two ​Clubs** ​— ‌“Chaser” ​and ​“Driver”, ‌the magic ​clubs ​Baʿal ‌threw ​to ‌shatter ​his skull ​— ​the ​cycle’s ‌most ‌quoted ​scene.
- **The ‌Divine ​Council** ​— ‌He ‌demanded ‌Baʿal’s ‌surrender from ​the ‌council ​of ​El; ​the ‌gods’ cowardice ​set ​the ​war ‌in ​motion.
- ​**The Tablet’s ​Return** ‌— ​Found ‌at ​Ugarit ‌(Ras ​Shamra) in ‌1929 ‌— ​the ​Baal ​Cycle ​restored Canaanite ‌religion ‌to ​history.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Yammu’s mythology ​is the Baal Cycle’s ‌opening act: the ‌sea demands the storm-god’s ​surrender, the council ​wavers, and Baʿal — ​armed by the ​craftsman-god Kothar-wa-Khasis with two ​magic clubs — ‌goes out to meet ​the flood and ​splits the sea’s skull ‌between the eyes. ​It is the Levant’s ‌own dragon-combat — ​the same pattern as ‌Marduk and Tiamat, ​Indra and Vritra, told ​in the oldest ​alphabetic literature on earth.[^1]

### ​The Embassy of ​the Sea (KTU 1.2)

‌The cycle opens with ​Yammu’s envoys at ‌the divine council, demanding ​that Baʿal be ‌delivered into the sea’s ​power. El, the ‌aged king of the ​gods, wavers — ‌and it is left ​to Baʿal himself, ​with Kothar-wa-Khasis’s weapons, to ‌answer the demand. ‌The scene sets the ‌cycle’s whole theology: ​kingship is taken, not ​granted.[^2]

### The Two ‌Magic Clubs (KTU 1.2 ​iv)

Kothar-wa-Khasis gives ​Baʿal two clubs — ‌Yaggarish, “Chaser”, and ​Ayyamarri, “Driver”. Baʿal strikes ​Yammu between the ‌eyes, on the skull: ​‘Yammu is dead! ‌Baʿal is king!’ The ​lines are the ​Levantine storm-god’s coronation — ​and the pattern ​that Hebrew poetry would ‌echo in its ‌own sea-combat, Yahweh versus ​Yam.

### Yam in ‌the Psalms (Biblical Echoes)

​The Hebrew Bible ​keeps the sea-god’s name ‌as a common ‌noun and his defeat ‌as a motif: ‌‘Thou didst divide the ​sea (yam) by ‌thy strength’, ‘thou rulest ​the raging of ​the sea (yam)’. The ​Ugaritic tablets revealed ‌what the Psalms were ​arguing against — and ​what they preserved: ​Yammu’s defeat is the ‌Old Testament sea’s ​backstory.

### The Sea-Enemy Pattern ​(Comparative Frame)

Yammu ​belongs to the oldest ‌myth-complex in the ​lexicon: the storm-god versus ‌the sea. Tiamat ​and Marduk in Babylon, ‌Vritra and Indra ​in the Rigveda, Typhon ‌and Zeus in ‌Greece — the pattern ​crosses the whole ​ancient world, and the ​Ugaritic telling is ​among its most vivid ‌witnesses. The sea ‌is always first, and ​always beaten.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Yammu ​is ‌the Canaanite ‌branch ​of ​the ​ancient ​Near Eastern ​sea-enemy ‌— ​Tiamat’s ​cousin, with ‌the ​Babylonian ‌goddess-dragon ​as his ‌nearest ​kin. ​The ​Hebrew ​tradition suppressed ​him ‌into ​a ‌noun but ​kept ‌his ​combat; ‌and ​modern study ‌of ​the ​Baal ‌Cycle restored ‌him ‌as ​the ​indispensable witness ‌to ​what ​Israel’s ‌religion ​argued with. ​The ‌Greeks ​of ‌the coast ​heard ​Poseidon ​in ​him; ‌the scholars ‌hear ​the ‌pattern.[^1]

​Kindred figures ​in ‌the ‌PuniCodex ‌cross-tradition index ‌include ​[[angrboda|Angrboða]] ‌(chaos ​/ ​primordial / ​world ‌serpent), ​[[apep|ꜥꜣpp]] ​(chaos / ​primordial ‌/ ​world ​serpent), ​[[aseratu|Ašeratu]] (sea ‌/ ​water), ‌[[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]] ​(sea / ‌water), ​[[benzaiten|Benzaiten]] ‌(sea ‌/ water), ​and ​[[chaos|Cháos]] ​(chaos ​/ ‌primordial / ‌world ​serpent).

sections.label: Phoenician Inscriptions
sections.body:
Phoenician inscriptions from the Levant, Cyprus, and the Mediterranean diaspora preserve theonyms and titles relevant to Yammu. The consonantal Phoenician script leaves vowel quality to interpretation.

The restored form Yammu represents scholarly vocalization of those consonantal texts.[^1]

sections.label: Biblical References
sections.body:
The Hebrew Bible preserves encounters with Phoenician/Canaanite religious culture, including references to figures related to Yammu. Biblical polemic and narrative preserve the name for later readers.

The Unicode restoration Yammu marks the scholarly vocalized form.[^1]

sections.label: Classical Sources
sections.body:
Classical Greek and Latin authors — Philo of Byblos, Eusebius, and others — transmit Phoenician theogonic traditions about Yammu. These secondary sources filter the material through Greco-Roman interpretive categories.

The restored spelling Yammu anchors the name in modern scholarship.[^1]
